title: 1 Kings 12:1–15
context: After Solomon’s death, Israel gathers at Shechem to make Rehoboam king and asks him, with Jeroboam present, to lighten the heavy yoke of labor Solomon imposed. Rehoboam rejects the elders’ counsel of servant leadership and follows his young companions’ harsh advice. The narrator adds that this was brought about from the LORD to fulfill Ahijah’s word. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about wise and foolish leadership, affirming God’s providence and Rehoboam’s responsibility together.

verses.text: Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had come to Shechem to make him king.
verses.arminianNotes:
Rehoboam goes to Shechem, where all Israel has gathered to make him king. The setting is significant.

Arminian readers see the northern tribes expecting a say in their king’s terms.
verses.reformedNotes:
Shechem had a long history, including covenant renewal under Joshua (Joshua 24) and Abimelech’s failed kingship (Judges 9).

Reformed readers see a place where loyalty to God had been publicly tested before. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting the stakes of the gathering.

verses.text: When Jeroboam the son of Nebat heard of it (for he was yet in Egypt, where he had fled from the presence of King Solomon, and Jeroboam lived in Egypt;
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeroboam hears of it while still in Egypt, where he had fled from Solomon. The narrative connects the two stories.

Arminian readers see Jeroboam positioned to respond when the time comes.
verses.reformedNotes:
The parenthetical note reminds readers of 11:40. Jeroboam’s return is imminent.

Reformed readers see providence bringing the announced leader back at the right moment. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, without assuming details of Jeroboam’s movements beyond what the text gives.

verses.text: and they sent and called him), Jeroboam and all the assembly of Israel came, and spoke to Rehoboam, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel sends for Jeroboam, and he and the assembly come to speak to Rehoboam. The northern tribes act together.

Arminian readers see the people taking initiative to seek relief through negotiation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jeroboam stands with the assembly. The request will be made publicly.

Reformed readers see events moving toward the fulfillment of Ahijah’s word. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note that the people approach Rehoboam with a request rather than open revolt.

verses.text: “Your father made our yoke difficult. Now therefore make the hard service of your father, and his heavy yoke which he put on us, lighter, and we will serve you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
They ask Rehoboam to lighten the heavy yoke and hard service Solomon placed on them, and they will serve him. Their request is reasonable.

Arminian readers see an opportunity for wise, servant-hearted leadership.
verses.reformedNotes:
The complaint concerns forced labor and taxation. The people offer loyalty in return for relief.

Reformed readers see a just appeal to a new king. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the responsibilities of rulers toward their people.

verses.text: He said to them, “Depart for three days, then come back to me.” So the people departed.
verses.arminianNotes:
Rehoboam tells them to return in three days. He takes time to decide.

Arminian readers see a real decision lying before the king. The outcome is not yet settled. Rehoboam has time to weigh his answer carefully.
verses.reformedNotes:
The delay allows consultation. Rehoboam will seek advice.

Reformed readers see the king’s choice unfolding within God’s purpose. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, noting that the next verses present Rehoboam with two very different paths.

verses.text: King Rehoboam took counsel with the old men who had stood before Solomon his father while he yet lived, saying, “What counsel do you give me to answer these people?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Rehoboam consults the old men who served Solomon, asking how to answer the people. He begins wisely.

Arminian readers see the value of experienced counsel offered to a new king.
verses.reformedNotes:
The elders had served under Solomon and know the kingdom. Their perspective is seasoned.

Reformed readers see wisdom available to Rehoboam. Both traditions read this as shared ground about seeking counsel, and note that Proverbs often commends many counselors (for example, Proverbs 15:22).

verses.text: They replied, “If you will be a servant to this people today, and will serve them, and answer them with good words, then they will be your servants forever.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The elders advise him to serve the people and speak good words, and they will serve him forever. Servant leadership is their counsel.

Arminian readers see wisdom that echoes later teaching about servant leadership (compare Mark 10:42–45).
verses.reformedNotes:
The advice is humble and practical. Kindness would secure loyalty.

Reformed readers see godly wisdom in the elders’ words. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about leadership that serves rather than dominates.

verses.text: But he abandoned the counsel of the old men which they had given him, and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him, who stood before him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Rehoboam abandons the elders’ counsel and consults the young men who grew up with him. He turns away from wisdom.

Arminian readers see a free choice with serious consequences. He chooses familiar voices over wise ones.
verses.reformedNotes:
The king prefers his peers to experienced advisers. The narrator marks the turning point.

Reformed readers see folly chosen over wisdom. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting that the choice is Rehoboam’s own even as it serves the fulfillment of God’s word (12:15).

verses.text: He said to them, “What counsel do you give, that we may answer these people who have spoken to me, saying, ‘Make the yoke that your father put on us lighter’?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Rehoboam asks the young men how to answer the people’s request for a lighter yoke. He seeks a second opinion.

Arminian readers see Rehoboam inclined toward a different answer than the elders gave.
verses.reformedNotes:
The repetition of the people’s words keeps the issue clear. The king wants a different response.

Reformed readers see the heart seeking counsel that confirms its preference. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground about the danger of choosing advisers who will say what one wants to hear.

verses.text: The young men who had grown up with him said to him, “Tell these people who spoke to you, saying, ‘Your father made our yoke heavy, but make it lighter to us’—tell them, ‘My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist.
verses.arminianNotes:
The young men tell him to say, “My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist.” Their advice is arrogant.

Arminian readers see pride offered as strength. Their words reveal more about their hearts than about strength.
verses.reformedNotes:
The image boasts of greater power than Solomon. It is meant to intimidate.

Reformed readers see arrogance that ignores the people’s burden. Both traditions read this as shared ground, recognizing the folly of leadership that answers grievance with threats.

verses.text: Now my father burdened you with a heavy yoke, but I will add to your yoke. My father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
They urge him to promise a heavier yoke and harsher discipline: ‘scorpions’ instead of whips. The language is harsh.

Arminian readers see the young men encouraging cruelty. Such counsel treats the people as subjects to be crushed rather than served.
verses.reformedNotes:
‘Scorpions’ is a vivid image for severe punishment; its exact meaning is uncertain.

Reformed readers see oppressive counsel. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, noting how sharply it contrasts with the elders’ advice of service and kindness in verse 7.

verses.text: So Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam the third day, as the king asked, saying, “Come to me again the third day.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeroboam and the people return on the third day as Rehoboam asked. The moment of decision arrives.

Arminian readers see the people keeping their part of the arrangement in good faith.
verses.reformedNotes:
The people come as instructed. The king must now answer.

Reformed readers see the scene set for the fulfillment of God’s word. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground and note the narrative’s building tension before Rehoboam’s reply.

verses.text: The king answered the people roughly, and abandoned the counsel of the old men which they had given him,
verses.arminianNotes:
The king answers roughly, abandoning the elders’ counsel. His tone matches his decision.

Arminian readers see Rehoboam freely choosing harshness over wisdom. His harsh words reflect the counsel he chose to follow, and they will cost him dearly.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator repeats that he rejected the elders’ advice. The decision is deliberate.

Reformed readers see folly displayed publicly. Both traditions read this as shared ground, holding Rehoboam fully responsible for the way he speaks to his people.

verses.text: and spoke to them according to the counsel of the young men, saying, “My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke. My father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Rehoboam speaks as the young men advised: he will add to their yoke and punish them with scorpions. The words are repeated.

Arminian readers see a ruler choosing domination over service.
verses.reformedNotes:
The king adopts the harsh counsel exactly. The repetition emphasizes his choice.

Reformed readers see arrogance leading to loss. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the folly of oppressive rule, which will cost Rehoboam most of his kingdom.

verses.text: So the king didn’t listen to the people; for it was a thing brought about from the LORD, that he might establish his word, which the LORD spoke by Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam the son of Nebat.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king did not listen to the people, for it was a thing brought about from the LORD to fulfill Ahijah’s word. Providence and choice meet.

Arminian readers see God directing Rehoboam’s freely chosen folly toward his announced purpose.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator explains the deeper cause: God was fulfilling his word to Jeroboam.

Reformed readers see God ordaining the outcome through Rehoboam’s responsible choice. Both traditions affirm providence and human responsibility here; their difference on such texts is treated at Judges 9:23.
